title: HTML Semantics and Document Structure
objectives: Explain what semantic HTML is and why it matters for accessibility, SEO and maintenance.
Use landmark elements (header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer) correctly.
Build a logical heading hierarchy and connect form inputs to labels.
Spot 'div soup' and non-semantic patterns in AI-generated markup.
Write a program that checks a heading outline for skipped levels.
definition: Semantic HTML means choosing elements for what content is, not how it looks: a navigation menu goes in nav, the primary content in main, a clickable action in button, and section titles in h1–h6. Browsers, search engines and assistive technologies such as screen readers use these meanings to understand and navigate the page. Styling is applied separately with CSS.

theory.heading: Why semantics matter
theory.body: A screen reader user can jump between headings, landmarks and form fields only if the markup exposes them. Search engines use headings and structure to understand topics. Developers read semantic markup faster because element names describe intent. AI assistants often generate nested divs with click handlers because that pattern is common in training data, so reviewing generated markup for semantics is a real interview topic.
points: Accessibility: built-in roles, keyboard behaviour and names come free with native elements.
SEO: clear structure helps crawlers understand the page.

theory.heading: Landmarks and sectioning elements
theory.body: Landmark elements divide a page into regions that assistive technology can list and jump to. header and footer hold introductory and closing content; nav holds major navigation links; main holds the unique primary content and should appear once per page; aside holds tangential content; article is self-contained content that could stand alone, such as a blog post or a product card; section groups related content that has its own heading.
points: <article> for independently distributable items; <section> for thematic groups with a heading.
Use <div> only when no semantic element fits, typically for styling wrappers.

theory.heading: Headings form an outline
theory.body: Headings h1 to h6 create the document outline that screen reader users navigate. Start with a single h1 describing the page, and go down one level at a time: an h2 followed directly by an h4 skips a level and suggests missing structure. Choose heading levels by structure, never by font size; change the size with CSS instead.
points: One h1 per page is the widely recommended convention.
Do not skip levels when going deeper (h2 -> h3, not h2 -> h4).
Going back up (h4 -> h2) is fine when a new section starts.

theory.heading: Interactive elements and forms
theory.body: Use <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation. A div with an onclick handler is not focusable with the keyboard and is not announced as a button. Every form control needs an accessible name, usually from a <label for> that matches the input's id. Native input types (email, tel, number, date) give mobile keyboards and basic validation for free.
points: Images need meaningful alt text, or alt="" if decorative.

theory.heading: The document skeleton
theory.body: Every page should declare <!DOCTYPE html> for standards mode, set lang on the html element so screen readers pronounce text correctly, declare UTF-8 encoding and include a responsive viewport meta tag. A descriptive <title> appears in tabs and search results. These lines are short but frequently missing from quick generated snippets.

example.title: Refactoring generated 'div soup' into semantic HTML
example.body: An assistant generated a header built from divs, with a clickable div as the menu button. The refactor uses header, nav, a real button and a list of links. Visual appearance can stay identical through CSS, but keyboard users can now tab to the button, screen readers announce a navigation landmark, and the code explains itself.

takeaways: Choose elements for meaning; style with CSS.
Landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) make pages navigable for assistive technology.
Use one h1 and do not skip heading levels when going deeper.
Use <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation, never clickable divs.
Every input needs a label; every meaningful image needs alt text.
Review AI-generated markup for div soup; it is a common weakness.

interview.question: What is semantic HTML?
interview.answer: Using HTML elements according to the meaning of the content, such as nav for navigation, button for actions and h1–h6 for headings, rather than generic divs and spans styled to look right.
interview.explanation: Add the benefits: accessibility, SEO and readable code.

interview.question: What is the difference between section, article and div?
interview.answer: article is self-contained content that makes sense on its own, like a post or a product card. section groups thematically related content, normally with a heading. div has no meaning and is used for layout or styling hooks when nothing else fits.
interview.explanation: Interviewers like the 'could it be syndicated on its own?' test for article.

interview.question: Why is <div onclick> a bad substitute for <button>?
interview.answer: A div is not focusable by keyboard, does not respond to Enter or Space, and is not announced as a button by screen readers. Recreating that needs tabindex, a role and key handlers, while <button> provides it all natively.
interview.explanation: This is the most common accessibility flaw in generated UIs, so mention you check for it in reviews.

interview.question: How should headings be structured on a page?
interview.answer: One h1 that describes the page, then h2 for main sections, h3 for subsections and so on, without skipping levels when going deeper. Levels reflect structure; visual size is controlled by CSS.
interview.explanation: Mention that screen reader users navigate by headings, which is why the outline matters.

interview.question: What would you check when reviewing an AI-generated form?
interview.answer: Each input has an associated label, appropriate input types and autocomplete attributes, a real submit button inside a form element, visible error messages tied to fields, and server-side validation in addition to any HTML validation.
interview.explanation: Linking client-side semantics to server-side validation shows full-stack awareness.

practice.title: Check a page's heading outline
practice.objective: Apply heading-hierarchy rules by building an outline and reporting structural problems.
practice.statement: Each input line is a heading such as 'h2 Courses'. Print the outline: each heading on its own line as '- <text>' indented by two spaces per level below h1. Then report issues in document order: the first heading is not h1 ('first heading is hN, expected h1'), a heading goes deeper by more than one level compared with the previous heading ('skipped from hA to hB at '<text>''), and every h1 after the first ('extra h1 '<text>''). Print each issue as 'Issue: <message>', then 'Result: OK' or 'Result: <n> issue(s)'.
practice.input_format: One heading per line: h1–h6 (case-insensitive), a space, then the heading text.
practice.output_format: The indented outline, then zero or more 'Issue: ...' lines, then the Result line.

example.input:
h1 Store
h2 Products
h4 Pricing
h1 Footer title
example.output:
- Store
  - Products
      - Pricing
- Footer title
Issue: skipped from h2 to h4 at 'Pricing'
Issue: extra h1 'Footer title'
Result: 2 issue(s)

constraints: Going up any number of levels (for example h4 to h2) is allowed.
explanation: Parse each line with a regular expression into a level (1–6) and text.
Print the outline with '  '.repeat(level - 1) so nesting is visible.
Only the first heading is checked against h1; later headings are compared with the previous level.
A jump deeper by more than one level is a skip; moving back up is allowed.
Count h1 elements and flag every one after the first, then print the summary.

quiz.question: Which element should wrap the primary, unique content of a page?
quiz.explanation: <main> is the landmark for the page's primary content and should appear once.

quiz.question: What is the main accessibility problem with this markup?
options: It cannot be focused or activated with the keyboard and is not announced as a button
The class name is too short
onclick only works in older browsers
quiz.explanation: Native <button> provides focus, keyboard activation and the button role; a div provides none of these.

quiz.question: A designer wants a sub-section title to look small. The structure calls for an h2. What should you do?
options: Use a bold <span> instead of a heading
Keep the h2 and reduce its size with CSS
Use an h5 because it is smaller
quiz.explanation: Heading level reflects structure; visual size is a CSS concern.

quiz.question: How is an input most reliably given an accessible name?
options: A title attribute on the form
Bold text placed next to the input
A <label> whose for attribute matches the input's id
quiz.explanation: An associated label provides a persistent accessible name and enlarges the click target. Placeholders disappear when typing.

quiz.question: A product listing shows many independent product cards that could each be shared on their own. Which element suits each card?
quiz.explanation: <article> represents self-contained content that makes sense independently, like a product card or post.
